maintopic: ACTION OF PROTECTIVE STAFF RESPECTING DELIVERY OF CERTAIN DOCUMENTS TO PRESS GALLERY BY MR. ROGER JAY

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: ACTION OF PROTECTIVE STAFF RESPECTING DELIVERY OF CERTAIN DOCUMENTS TO PRESS GALLERY BY MR. ROGER JAY
speechtext:
Hon. members may be aware of the report that appeared in this morning's Globe and Mail-I believe the matter was also referred to during the CBC national newscast this morning-having to do with an incident which apparently occurred yesterday involving Mr. Roger Jay, communications officer for the Union of Ontario Indians, when he was delivering certain documents to the House of Commons. It was suggested in the press report and newscast that the gentleman had been treated unfairly in that certain comments had been made by the chief of the protective staff of the House of Commons. I might say I had a conversation this morning with the Sergeant-at-Arms who is responsible for the administration of the protective service. Later in the day he will give me a complete statement in regard to the matter and I will immediately report to the House.
I might say in a preliminary way that Chief Syms has given the assurance that he did not at any time pass any comment or judgment in relation to the contents of the statement proposed to be delivered. I want to assure hon. members, in any event, that I will certainly, on behalf of the House and on behalf of the staff of the House of Commons, extend apologies to this gentleman if in any way we have been at fault. Whether we are or not, we still express regret if any inconvenience was caused to this distinguished person who was here on official business and had every right to call on the press gallery as he proposed to do.
I think it would be unfair to our staff and to the chief if I said more until a formal report has been received which I will pass on to the House later today.

subtopic: B.C. INDIAN LAND QUESTION BILL PROVISION FOR RECOGNITION THAT ABORIGINAL AND HEREDITARY OWNERSHIP NOT EXTINGUISHED

speechtext: Mr. Thomas S. Barnett (Comox-Alberni), for Mr. Howard (Skeena), moved for leave to introduce Bill C-166, respecting Indian lands in the province of British Columbia.

subtopic: B.C. INDIAN LAND QUESTION BILL PROVISION FOR RECOGNITION THAT ABORIGINAL AND HEREDITARY OWNERSHIP NOT EXTINGUISHED
speechtext: Explain.

subtopic: B.C. INDIAN LAND QUESTION BILL PROVISION FOR RECOGNITION THAT ABORIGINAL AND HEREDITARY OWNERSHIP NOT EXTINGUISHED
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this bill is to give parliamentary recognition to the historical fact that the aboriginal and hereditary ownership of the land in what is now British Columbia has not been extinguished. The native Indian people in British Columbia have been concerned about this for many decades and have pressed their case before government without result.
Motion agreed to, bill read the first time and ordered to be printed.

SUGGESTED USE OF FOREIGN EXCHANGE RESERVES TO REGAIN CONTROL OF CERTAIN SECTORS, INCLUDING FOREIGN-CONTROLLED INSURANCE COMPANIES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Acting Prime Minister. In light of a government report released yesterday which revealed that Canada's foreign exchange reserves reached a record level of $5.67 billion in February, and in view of the fact that Canada has a floating dollar and hence does not need these reserves, does the government intend to use part of these funds in order to regain Canadian control of certain key sectors of the economy which are currently dominated by foreign firms?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: SUGGESTED USE OF FOREIGN EXCHANGE RESERVES TO REGAIN CONTROL OF CERTAIN SECTORS, INCLUDING FOREIGN-CONTROLLED INSURANCE COMPANIES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the hon. gentleman is suggesting we should keep our reserves in other than a liquid form. I would be glad to hear more details of his proposal.

subtopic: SUGGESTED USE OF FOREIGN EXCHANGE RESERVES TO REGAIN CONTROL OF CERTAIN SECTORS, INCLUDING FOREIGN-CONTROLLED INSURANCE COMPANIES
speechtext: That is precisely what is being suggested. To be more specific, in view of the report made available from Swiss sources earlier in the week that Canada has the highest percentage of foreign-controlled insurance companies, would the government consider seriously using part of its foreign exchange reserves in order to gain control of these foreign-owned insurance companies in Canada, bearing in mind that these companies are an important source of investment capital which could be used to make more jobs available in this country?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: SUGGESTED USE OF FOREIGN EXCHANGE RESERVES TO REGAIN CONTROL OF CERTAIN SECTORS, INCLUDING FOREIGN-CONTROLLED INSURANCE COMPANIES
speechtext: What the hon. gentleman is suggesting is that if we needed these reserves to support our currency we would sell these assets. I do not think that is a very good policy.

TORONTO-USE OF NEW FACILITY AS MAJOR TERMINAL FOR OVERSEAS FLIGHTS-POSSIBLE SEPARATION OF PASSENGER AND FREIGHT SERVICES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Transport concerning his announcement yesterday of a new airport in the Toronto region. Is it intended that the new airport will be the major terminal for overseas flights or will Malton continue in this role?

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald C. Jamieson (Minister oi Transport):
subtopic: TORONTO-USE OF NEW FACILITY AS MAJOR TERMINAL FOR OVERSEAS FLIGHTS-POSSIBLE SEPARATION OF PASSENGER AND FREIGHT SERVICES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the new airport which I announced yesterday will be an international airport and will in fact be about comparable in size and operation as the one that is now under construction at Ste. Scholastique. As to whether it will be a totally international airport or one with a mix of services, this can, of course, only be determined with the passage of time. But it will have all the necessary amenities and facilities to be an international airport, and we visualize that that would be its main purpose.

subtopic: TORONTO-USE OF NEW FACILITY AS MAJOR TERMINAL FOR OVERSEAS FLIGHTS-POSSIBLE SEPARATION OF PASSENGER AND FREIGHT SERVICES
speechtext: Does the development of new airports in the Toronto and Montreal regions indicate a new policy concerning air traffic handling and, specifically, the development of a distinction between passengers and air freight?

subtopic: TORONTO-USE OF NEW FACILITY AS MAJOR TERMINAL FOR OVERSEAS FLIGHTS-POSSIBLE SEPARATION OF PASSENGER AND FREIGHT SERVICES
speechtext: No, Mr. Speaker. I do not expect, at least in the state of the art as it is at the moment, that there would be any such clearcut division. Generally speaking, air freight is carried quite frequently on planes that also carry passengers, and this looks as though it will be the largest part of such movements for the immediate future. So there could be no such distinction. Each of the airports at Toronto and Montreal is designed to accommodate the traffic growth that has taken place and will take place in both these regions.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I direct a question to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce. With the renewal of the United States-Canada trade discussions expected soon, can the minister say whether the United States government is still insisting on Canada increasing the duty free allowance on goods that Canadian tourists bring back from the United States?

Of course, my hon. friend knows that the Americans had identified as an irritant the fact that our allowances for tourists were lower than theirs in the first place, and had not been restored to the level they were in 1962 when we had to change them because of balance of payments difficulties. This was one of the irritants on which we had sympathy for the U.S. case.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: U.S. INSISTENCE ON INCREASE IN DUTY FREE ALLOWANCE ON GOODS PURCHASED BY CANADIANS- PROMOTION OF TRAVEL WITHIN CANADA

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS ACT. AUTHORIZATION OF FISCAL PAYMENTS TO AND TAX COLLECTION AGREEMENTS WITH PROVINCES

speechtext: The House resumed, from Thursday, March 2, consideration of the motion of Mr. Turner (Ottawa-Carleton) that Bill C-8, to authorize the making of certain fiscal payments to provinces, to authorize the entry into tax collection agreements with provinces, and to amend the Established Programs (Interim Arrangements) Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs.

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS ACT. AUTHORIZATION OF FISCAL PAYMENTS TO AND TAX COLLECTION AGREEMENTS WITH PROVINCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, during my remarks last night I indicated my support, and that of other hon. members of the New Democratic Party, for the principle of equalization. I said that this bill goes a long way towards implementation of the principle of equalization and that we were happy to see the progress, as indicated in this bill, made in effecting an effective equalization plan across Canada. At the same time it must also be said that I am very much alarmed, as are many people, by the prospect of certain proposals which, by one means or another, may undermine the principle of equalization. Any set of proposals which may attempt to declare the principle of equalization as unconstitutional or which may try to destroy the principle will bring about, if accepted, the greatest possible mischief to the well-being of Canada in the long run. Certainly I, for one, want to make sure that all steps are taken to ensure that the principle of equalization is not destroyed or undermined and that this
Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements mischief never comes about. Even though some of the proposals brought forward as alternatives to the present system may be well meaning, I think they are ill-conceived and will not achieve the objectives set for them by their proponents.
Last night in my remarks I also urged the government to take steps to broaden the revenue base in determining equalization payments and to include within the scope of the calculations and the formula used for determining the revenue base the matter of municipal revenues. This is particularly important at this time because shifts in responsibilities with regard to various government functions are taking place as between the provincial and municipal levels of government. A number of developments are taking place in various provinces which contain implications for an adequate equalization plan across Canada.
I am also concerned about the future of our health programs, and especially about federal participation in those programs. It seems to me, on the basis of certain indications which are evident at present, that the federal government is making moves in an effort to opt out of these programs in the long run. The first step in the process, of course, is limiting the federal government's contribution to these programs. As I understand the situation, the federal government has proposed that further increases in federal contributions to health programs, and federal-provincial health programs in particular, involving hospitalization and medical care, should be based upon growth in the gross national product or some other similar indicator.
Actually, health costs at present are growing more quickly than these indicators. Therefore, the government's proposal will leave the provinces holding the bag, so to speak. At the same time I think we should all be concerned about increases in health costs and also remember that we must reorganize some of our health delivery systems in Canada, while making sure at the same time that we do not decrease the quality of health care. Actually, we must take steps to improve the quality of health care across Canada. I suggest that this can only be achieved if the federal government makes it clear that it will go along with the provinces and stand behind the provinces in supporting these programs, both at present and in future.
Today, Mr. Speaker, I want to refer to some further points that are of concern in our consideration of this bill. I wish to make particular reference to some remarks the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) made in introducing the bill. At one point in his speech the minister referred to the benefits of stabilization and the changes made in stabilization payments. He said, as recorded at page 435 of Hansard:
Another benefit of stabilization is the help it provides to provinces when they attempt to borrow on international money markets.
The minister's statement, Mr. Speaker, may be perfectly correct. Yet it seems to me that that statement conflicts with the request that the federal government some time ago made of the provinces when it asked them to refrain as much as possible from entering the international money markets in raising money for their financial

March 3, 1972
Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements
requirements. The minister also made the following statement as recorded on the same page of Hansard:
Within this framework of tax harmonization and uniformity, provinces are perfectly free to establish their own rates of taxation. They have been doing so to an increasing extent. This is the real test of fiscal independence and decentralization-the willingness to exercise the responsibility to tax as well as the responsibility to spend.
I must take issue with that statement, Mr. Speaker. Although we may recognize that, technically, within the present restricted framework the statement is accurate, there are also loopholes in it. At present the provinces can be involved in the system of taxation as proposed only if they accept the basic structure proposed by the federal government with respect to tax systems. They can then determine at what percentage level they want to have their taxes. However, they must accept the federal government's basic structure as it has been established. If one province wants to give greater benefits and exemptions to lower income groups, for example, they are not able to do so under the present plan. This is a real deficiency. I recognize that there are complexities in overcoming this problem, but I do not think it is fair to say that provinces are perfectly free to establish their own rates of taxation when they have to conduct themselves within the type of framework that has been imposed by the federal government.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) made another statement which is recorded on the same page of Hansard. The minister stated:
The present bill would also empower the federal government to collect, on behalf of Manitoba, Saskatchewan, and the four Atlantic provinces the succession duties which they have proposed. I want to emphasize that these provinces have made the decision to rejoin Ontario, Quebec and British Columbia in the succession duty field entirely on their own. We have had no part in their decision and have agreed to assist in collections only in response to their urgent requests to us.
That is a nice way for the minister to wash his hands of the entire area of succession duties, as the provinces are now taking them up. The federal government must take primary responsibility for this development. In fact, it was the federal government that opted out of the estate tax field in the income tax bill which was passed in the last session. The federal government must assume primary responsibility for the many problems that are going to arise with regard to the entire matter of handling estate and succession duties. In many cases, the provinces have no choice but to enter this field for purposes of obtaining revenue and so on. In fact, the federal government has recognized this in the definition of revenue sources, since they have included a reference to succession duties in the formula. The federal government has done a great disservice to Canada by opting out of the field of taxation of estates or any form of imposition of succession duties. One way to keep this country together, about which the government claims it is so concerned, is to ensure that there is one levy across Canada with regard to taxation of estates. That levy can most properly be imposed by the federal government.
Many inequities will very shortly develop. The new situation is such that nine out of 10 provinces will be in the

succession duty field. The province of Alberta thinks it will get away with something by staying out of this field. In the long run, it may find that it will be faced with some serious problems. What is the situation with regard to some cases? In recent months some very well known and distinguished Canadians have passed away, leaving large estates. They happened to live in the provinces of Ontario and Quebec. Under the new plan, those provinces will be the sole beneficiaries of most of the succession duties of the estates of these people. In some cases these individuals gained their wealth and financial resources by carrying on business activity all across Canada, not just in the particular province in which they lived.
If the federal government is really concerned with the principle of equalization as a means of keeping Canada together, it has a duty to take the initiative and once again re-enter the field of taxation of estates by imposing an equitable succession duty, the revenue from which could be distributed among the provinces on an equitable formula. The only type of equitable plan in the long run will result from the federal government accepting its responsibility in this field.
I want to associate myself with the remarks of the hon. member for Waterloo (Mr. Saltsman). He stressed the importance of the equalization of transportation costs in Canada in the future. This is one of the thrusts that should be developed in federal policy in the coming years. Moves toward equalization of transportation costs would do a great deal to keep Canada together. This one step would do more to eliminate regional disparities in Canada than the millions of dollars which the federal government is handing to private industry and private business. Transportation costs is one of the major factors contributing to regional disparity in Canada at the present time.
I suggest this factor is important in relation to some of the comments made recently by the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin) when he indicated he and his department are working on an industrial strategy for Canada. If the benefits of this new industrial strategy, whatever it is going to be, are to be equitably distributed across Canada, it will be necessary to ensure there is an equalization of transportation costs. With the technology and economics of the operations of many industries in Canada today, if we allow the present inequitable transportation cost structure to remain, many parts of Canada will be left out in the cold when this new industrial strategy unfolds.
While a good many aspects of the bill before us are concerned with economic measures and financial aspects of the operation of government, there are some features which deserve attention. Under this bill there is another five year extension of the Hospital Insurance Act, the Blind Persons Act, the Disabled Persons Act, the Unemployment Assistance Act and the Canada Assistance Plan. They are simply being extended for another five years. It is not clear whether there will be any changes or improvements in these programs. I certainly feel we should give them some consideration.
Today I would like to mention two particular areas which I feel should be kept in mind. First, I want to make particular reference to the Blind Persons Act. This is a selective program to assist people with a particular prob-
March 3, 1972

lem in life. It is not the type of selective program that tells the people concerned that they will receive more favourable treatment than other groups in society. Under the terms and benefits of this act, blind people today are in a selective unfavourable position. It is a disgrace that we in Canada have been so niggardly in our assistance to the blind people in this country. I hope the federal government will take some initiative to improve the level of assistance provided to this group of people.
I also note that the Canada Assistance Plan is to be extended another five years. There are many worthwhile features in the Canada Assistance Plan in terms of the federal government's contribution to this program. There are deficiencies as well. I wish to make just one comment in this regard. That is to take note of the recent growth of unfavourable comment in Canada about welfare programs in general. There seems to be a mood and feeling developing in Canada that there are many thousands of bums, people who are too lazy to go out and work and so on. They feel they are simply getting along on the Canada Assistance Plan benefits and that the whole program is a shambles. I suggest we all have to recognize that some problems do exist. We all recognize that there are new life styles and new life patterns developing in Canada. These are producing problems which have not been totally taken into account in the programs as they have been developed in this area to date.
But if we concentrate our attention in this area without reference to those who have a justifiable claim to assistance we are doing a disservice to many thousands who are in dire need. A good case could be made out for a better deal for many who are presently existing on welfare benefits under the Canada Assistance Plan and various provincial plans. We need to keep in mind our responsibility as a nation to help those who are not able to help themselves adequately. It may be we are devoting insufficient attention to the requirements of many thousands who are living in unfortunate circumstances and who have a justifiable claim for assistance under these programs.
The government and its officials will feel a justifiable sense of accomplishment with respect to the bill now before us. There are useful items in it. Some progress has been made in implementing the principle of equalization though much work remains to be done. I certainly hope we shall see more progress in the coming months in dealing with some of the shortcomings which have been pointed out in the course of this debate.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is not the type of speech I prefer to make in this House or anywhere else for that matter. I intend to deal with some of the less lovely aspects of political life. I am dealing with the subject of irresponsible statements made by some British Columbia politicians who are in a position to know better and who are, to put it plainly, making pronouncements aimed at showing that French-speaking Canadians are being favoured by the present federal government.
Before going further, I should like to say that the remarks I intend to make are not directed against members of the British Columbia Legislative Assembly whose
Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements
ridings are in my federal constituency of Coast-Chilcotin, namely, Alex Fraser of the Social Credit party, the member for Cariboo; the Hon. Isabel Dawson, Minister without Portfolio, the member for Mackenzie; Bill Hartley of the NDP, the member for Yale-Lillooet, or Alan Williamson of the Liberal party, the member for West Vancouver. I am personally acquainted with these four people and I know that the type of campaign of which I am speaking would be beneath their dignity. As for some of the other members of the British Columbia Social Credit party, if the cap fits, let them wear it. But they should not think that because some of their wild statements are not always promptly rebutted here they have gone unnoticed. They are not unnoticed. There are letters. There are meetings arranged but never held. There are public statements. And they are on the record.
In this bill we are dealing with an idea which is fundamental to a federal state. Nothing could be more so. No nation can exist without brotherhood, without sharing and without recognition of the basic principle that the poorer sections of the nation shall be helped by those which are wealthier. There is nothing unfamiliar about that idea, whether we look to Yugoslavia or Switzerland or to a score of other states. And the complaints which arise in connection with redistribution are familiar enough, also.
I had the privilege during the recess of sitting in the famous mother of parliaments in Westminster. On the day I happened to be there, the British minister of trade and commerce was being questioned by the opposition and by members of his own party on his policies. The subject turned to special incentive grants to slow growth areas of Britain, and the familiar complaints were heard. Why is one particular area of Scotland receiving aid while certain areas of Wales or the Midlands are not? The old questions and the old problems. We in this federal parliament are engaged in trying to make some redistribution of the tax dollars of all Canadians in the name of a greater Canada. Skillfully or otherwise, this is what we are attempting to do. I am one who has some doubts about the ways in which federal governments, both this one and its many predecessors, have sought to redistribute the wealth. Also, as a westerner, I have some quarrels with the east. There are many of us at home who have no deep and abiding affection for the Canadian banking system, controlled, as it is, by eastern Canada-surely one of the most conservative and unimaginative banking systems of any vigorous young nation. We do not particularly appreciate the control of many of our companies by boards of directors selected from the east all of whom appear to have snow-white hair and ideas which are very old.
British Columbia is producing some of the wealth which is available for redistribution to the poorer provinces. This is being created back home by people with imagination, drive and energy and we sometimes feel we are doing it in spite of the eastern Canadian majority vote in this federation. But that is not the main burden of my remarks today. The fact remains that some redistribution of wealth is fundamental to the very existence of Canada. Indeed, the principle applies even within provinces. In the Province of British Columbia wealth tends to concentrate in the City of Vancouver. Provincial governments over the

March 3, 1972
Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements decades have ensured that some of this money is spread abroad to less developed areas of the province.
In any case, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) set out very clearly, using figures which I truly hope the newspapers of British Columbia will relay to their readers, the facts about the present redistribution system and its true proportions. Mr. Speaker, I am afraid I must deal openly here with a campaign which is being carried on by some people designed to convince the public that these transfers of money are not really from the richer to the poorer provinces but from the English-speaking provinces to the French-speaking province of Quebec. Nothing could be more divisive or unfair or damaging. Here today I should like to pass on a few balsawood cannonballs to any at home who wish to pursue this little game.
To illustrate my point, I have here some figures concerning the DREE program. They concern the grants made available under this legislation up to November 30, 1971, the latest date for which figures are available. They show that Quebec got by far the largest share of these grants-$86,299,232. Ontario received only $19,147,632, and British Columbia a mere $2,719,263. Now, any who wish to pursue the anti-French campaign in British Columbia are welcome to use those figures. However, those same people should not read any further in the Hansard report of this speech. They should confine themselves to the figures I mentioned a moment ago.
A misleading campaign of this sort is dependent on the suspension of curiosity on the part of the listener. I say this because the figures I quoted compare grants province by province, not person by person. To accept the proposition that Quebec gets the lion's share of these grants, it is essential that the audience never be reminded that Quebec has a larger population than almost all other provinces, not to mention a larger share of unemployment than many.
If we see what these grants amount to on a citizen to citizen rather than province to province basis, an entirely different picture emerges. Let us see what it is. The highest per capita grants go to Nova Scotia at $32.60 per person. The population of the province at the last census was 756,039, and the total grants amounted to $24,547,833. The second largest per capita grants went to New Brunswick, at $29.78 per capita. This is derived from a population figure of 616,788, with total grants of $18,368,467. Third in rank, for some reason, is the comparatively wealthy province of Alberta, one of the have provinces, at $16.40 per capita, grants totalling $23,999,555 and a population of 1,463,203. So far the charge of favouritism to French-speaking Canadians is not holding up very well, is it, Mr. Speaker? However, Quebec, which has a four-to-one ratio of French-speaking citizens, does rank fourth on the list. Industries there have had money made available to them at the rate $14.93 per capita, a little less than half the per capita rate for Nova Scotia. The total grants to Quebec were $86,299,232, with a population of 5,780,845.
I will run through the other provinces very briefly for hon. members. They can do their own arithmetic, but I can assure them that I have checked the figures very carefully. In diminishing order of amount we have New-

foundland with $12.54 per capita, total grants of $6,185,743 and a population of 493,396. Manitoba has $12 per capita, total grants of $11,572,647 with a population of 963,066. Prince Edward Island has $10.25 per capita, total grants of $1,112,727 and a population of 108,535. Saskatchewan has $5.87 per capita, total grants of $5,605,658 and a population of 955,344. Ontario has $2.75 per capita, total grants of $19,147,632 and a population of 6,960,870. Then lastly, British Columbia has $1.45 per capita, total grants of $2,719,263 and a population of 1,873,874.
I suggest there is much scope for debate about the picture that emerges here. One might wonder why Alberta, one of the three have provinces, ranks third while the other two have provinces of Ontario and British Columbia are ninth and tenth on the list. Or why the disparity between two neighbouring and very similar provinces, Saskatchewan and Manitoba? But that is not the purpose of these remarks. The purpose is to match the figures against claims that the federal government favours those Canadians who speak French. Let us keep that insinuation out of this debate and, hopefully, out of other political arenas.
To the extent that I can claim to know something about my home province, I want to tell the House that we British Columbians have our disagreements with the east and I suppose will continue to do so until, as is inevitable, the dumbbell shaped economy develops in Canada, as happened in the United States with the relationship of California and New York. But British Columbians in an overwhelming majority do not want to see federalism damaged by the insinuation that there is favouritism that is based upon whether a Canadian speaks French or English. I thank hon. members for their courteous attention.

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS ACT. AUTHORIZATION OF FISCAL PAYMENTS TO AND TAX COLLECTION AGREEMENTS WITH PROVINCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my colleagues have dealt ably with many aspects of this important legislation, and I intend to confine myself to one point and one point only. So that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) does not remain in a state of expectancy, it arises from clauses 9 and 10 whereby the federal government, on behalf of certain provincial governments, will collect succession duties under legislation that is still not passed in those provinces.
The federal authority, as 1 shall prove, has already frozen, in effect, the estates in those six Canadian provinces, and the argument I will be making is the very age-old one of taxation without legislation. It is true that ministers of finance are able to announce tax changes at certain times during the year, such as in their budget speeches, and the hours at which those taxes are to take effect are later given legislative authority.
However, once in a while a storm breaks in this institution as a result of different courses being followed. For example, a present judge of the Supreme Court of Canada, who previously was a Minister of Finance, Judge Abbott, provoked such a storm in the late forties by announcing an important tax change through the medium of radio, an announcement that later became known as the "radio budget". There was some considerable discussion in the parliament of that time as to whether this was the proper course to follow.
March 3, 1972

But if it is bad to have that sort of thing happening, it is much worse when we are wielding the headman's axe on behalf of other authorities. The Minister of Finance and the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Gray), whose department is mixed up in this unholy business, find themselves doing this chore on behalf of the provinces, none of whose legislatures, as far as I am aware, have yet passed the necessary legislation envisaged by this bill.
Clause 9 of the bill provides:
Where a province imposes duties or taxes on any legacy, succession, inheritance or gift, the Minister, with the approval of the Governor in Council, may on behalf of the Government of Canada enter into a tax collection agreement with the government of the province pursuant to which the Government of Canada will collect the provincial duties or taxes on behalf of the province and will make payments to the province in respect of the duties or taxes so collected in accordance with such terms and conditions as the agreement prescribes.
Subclause (2) provides that:
The Minister, with the approval of the Governor in Council, may on behalf of the Government of Canada enter into an agreement amending the terms and conditions of an agreement entered into pursuant to subsection (1).
The third subclause then provides that the federal authorities will not be bound by this type of agreement in the case of any death occurring after the year 1974. Already an apparatus has been set up for the collection of succession duties, or for what I call the freezing of estates. At least that is what I called it in a question that I put to the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Gray) the other day. A procedure has been devised and is being enforced by the banks, or really in effect being enforced by the local offices of the Department of National Revenue. This has the effect of subjecting the estates of people who have died since January 1 of this year to a new tax that has not yet been sanctioned or passed by any provincial legislature.
Up to the present the federal authority has been the one that has taken any discredit or any blame from people concerned, lawyers acting on behalf of estates, or widows and other beneficiaries of estates who find they are operating in the dark. And darkness is what it is, Mr. Speaker, because none of the legislatures have passed succession duty legislation. There have been press releases issued by the different ministers of finance of the provinces indicating what they will attempt to do in their legislature. But thanks to the public discussion that these releases have caused, for example in my own province of Nova Scotia, there are indications that the original proposals by the provincial ministers will be watered down, and that substantial changes will take place in what they announced just before the end of the past year. As a result, the federal authority comes under fire, and I think just fire, for taking part in such an exercise.
The federal authority opened the way to a lot of goodwill by reason of the very sensible provision it included in the income tax legislation upon which we spent so much time last fall and last December. A lot of good will was created by the removal of the estate tax, because very properly it was recognized that when certain estates were sold a form of capital gains tax would attach anyway. I believe that decision was endorsed by all parties in this
Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements
House, except perhaps the NDP. I want to be fair, and I believe most hon. members thought the removal of the estate tax was a proper thing.
But no sooner had it cleansed its hands in that direction than the government then bloodied them in another direction, I suppose out of good nature because who wants to collect taxes? It has bloodied them by offering to do this job of collecting this tax on behalf of certain of the provinces. I have said that the machinery has been set up, and I will proceed to outline it for the record. The first part of it is a directive, or really a letter from J. C. Ruddy, Director of the Estate and Gift Tax Division of the Department of National Revenue, directed to the Secretary-Treasurer of the Canadian Bankers' Association.
I presume the purpose of sending this letter to Mr. J. F. Riegert was simply that the Canadian Bankers' Association in turn could pass it along as an aide-memoire or direction to banks that have to decide what to do with safety deposit box contents when some of their customers die. I will read pretty fully from Mr. Ruddy's letter in order to give the substantial parts of it. I quote:
This will confirm our recent conversation concerning the proposed succession duty Acts of the provinces of Newfoundland, Prince Edward Island, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Manitoba and Saskatchewan, which the Department of National Revenue- Taxation will be administering on behalf of these provinces. The Acts when enacted will apply in respect of the estate of any person who dies on or after January 1st, 1972.
Mr. Ruddy is not a member of any provincial legislature that I know of, and it is pretty obvious that he is taking that as a direction from whatever agreement has been made between his minister and the federal government on the one hand, and the provincial ministers of finance and their governments on the other hand.
Prior to the coming into force of the proposed succession duty Acts there will, of course, be requests from executors, beneficiaries, or their representatives of the estates of persons who die after 1971 for the transfer or payment over of the property of the deceased including the proceeds of life insurance and also for the release of the contents of safety deposit boxes and property held in custody by banks, trust companies and others.
In order to facilitate matters for estate representatives and beneficiaries in these circumstances, until the respective Acts are passed by the Provincial Legislatures and the official provincial consent forms become available, the Department will release assets on request, by way of a letter under the signature of the Estate Tax Auditor of the District Office which will be processing the provincial succession duty return in respect to the estate of the deceased. The amount and number of assets released for any estate however will be restricted.
I ask that hon. members note this sentence very carefully.
-will be restricted to ensure that sufficient assets remain unreleased in order to protect the revenue.
To protect whose revenue? It is to protect provincial revenues, Mr. Speaker.
A specimen copy of the letter (marked 1) which will be used is enclosed for your information.
I now turn immediately to that form letter. It bears the Coat of Arms of Canada. It is typewritten in English on one side and in French on the other, and the English side reads:
Re: Estate of-

March 3, 1972
Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements
And space is left to fill in the name of the deceased. Then, this appears:
Date of death-
And another space. The text reads:
We acknowledge receipt of your recent communication in which you requested consent to transfer assets of the above noted deceased.
On behalf of the Province of .... in relation to the proposed Succession Duty Act, as announced on December 29, 1971, we agree to the transfer, delivery or payment over of the following property:
Then, room is left to list the property. If the provinces are not ready with their forms and paraphernalia for the collection of these succession duties, it appears that the federal government has been very quick to get into the field with its own forms drawn up for the occasion. I now quote further from the letter:
The same procedure may be continued as under the Estate Tax Act by an individual or corporation, in transferring, delivering or paying over property of the deceased person situated in Canada or where the deceased was domiciled in Canada any superannuation or death benefits and any amount payable under a policy of insurance, without the Minister's consent providing notice is given to the Department of such payment. The Estate Tax form ET75 (Notice of Payment) may continue to be used for this purpose until the official comparative provincial form is available.
So, while Estate Tax Form ET75 is as dead as the dodo so far as estates are concerned from the first of this year, its soul goes marching on in its use for the collection of provincial succession duties. The letter continues:
The Department would like to have particulars of payments, if any, already made to date in respect of persons who died after 1971.
That provokes the thought that some crusty lawyer acting for an estate may very well ask, "On what authority do you base this sort of request?" At least until the provincial act is in the field, I would imagine that the Department of National Revenue would have to tread pretty tenderly because there is no ground at all on which they can make such a request.
The letter continues:
The release of a safety deposit box or other depository will also be dealt with by the issuance of a letter from the district office concerned. A specimen copy of the letter (marked No. 2) which will be used, is attached.
That one again bears the coat of arms of Canada and the reference to the Department of National Revenue. The reference to the name of the estate reads:
On behalf of the province of ..., in relation to the proposed Succession Duty Act as announced on December 29,1971 we agree to the above named Custodian or Lessor permitting the following property to be withdrawn or delivered to the Executor, Administrator, the Legal Representative or his authorized attorney or agent:
Then, there is a blank space which can be filled in with the material to be released.
The letter continues:
The depository, usually of course a bank or a trust company, is asked to continue as now for Estate Tax purposes to send a certified list of the contents of the depository to the relevant district taxation office, that is the office where the return in respect of the estate of the deceased will be filed. Upon receipt of

this list the matter of the release by the issuance of the above mentioned letter will be promptly dealt with by the District Office receiving it.
The Estate Tax procedure in these circumstances of requiring consent (form ET 76) to the preliminary opening of a safety deposit box or other depository to withdraw documents or of consent (form ET 77) to the opening of a safety deposit box or other depository for the listing of contents will be dispensed with until the date when the provincial acts are enacted. There may be withdrawn at any time without consent the following:
1.	Will or other testamentary writing of the deceased.
2.	Birth certificate.
3.	Marriage licence.
4.	Marriage contract.
5.	Title deed, lease, agreement for sale or deed of mortgage or hypothec relating to real property.
6.	Any deed, record or other document required in connection with the burial of the deceased.
Then, on the final page of his letter, Mr. Ruddy continues:
The district taxation offices of the Department where the respective provincial succession duty returns of information will be filed and processed are set out below. Requests for release of assets should, of course, be directed to the District Office where the return will be filed or has been filed.
Where the deceased died domiciled in the province of
Newfoundland, Prince Edward Island or Nova Scotia New Brunswick Manitoba Saskatchewan
District Office where return will be filed
Halifax, N.S.
Saint John, N.B. Winnipeg, Man. Regina, Sask.
The provisions, of course, of the Estate Tax Act do not apply in respect to the estate of any person who dies after 1971 and accordingly the consent requirements of this Act to the transfer of assets do not apply in respect to the assets of any such estate.
The letter is signed J. C. Ruddy, director, Estate and Gift Tax Division.
I put the letter on the record because it may be useful for members of parliament whose constituents are asking about what happens between the first of the year and the time that the six provincial legislatures act, and they may wonder what is involved. I will not claim that it creates all the hardship in the world, because it does provide for the release of assets and in the past there has always been a method of releasing assets so that widows and young people can obtain material from estates. But there might be a hardship should any of the provinces decide to tax estates that are left by one spouse to another. This was the cause of considerable difficulty in the past, but it was removed.
One of the great accomplishments, the only one of which I can think, of the just society was the Estate Tax Act which was passed in 1968. It removed tax from estates passing between husbands and wives. There were many horrendous examples in the past of widows who went practically barefoot because of the enormous amounts of succession duties that had to be paid on their husbands' large estates and the fact that the estates were not in liquid form. That problem was removed by the Estate Tax
March 3, 1972

Act in 1968, but it could return depending on what type of legislation is passed by the provincial legislatures. However, I will not get into that particular issue. It is the responsibility of these legislatures and I am sure they will fight those issues very capably. What I object to, however, is the fact that the federal authority is moving so willingly into the field. It is strange that they are going into a business that is bound to bring ridicule, hatred and contempt on their shoulders. It is strange to see that sort of thing happen, something which did not have to happen.
In my research into why we should be doing for others what, if we did it for ourselves, would get us into hot water-the word "we" refers to government-I went to the days of Charles I whose famous battle with Parliament over his right to taxation occurred in the seventeenth century. In 1628 the Petition of Right was: exhibited to His Majesty by the Lords Spiritual and Temporal, and Commons in this present Parliament assembled, concerning divers rights and liberties of the subjects-
To the King's most excellent Majesty: ... by which the statutes before mentioned, and other the good laws and statutes of this Realm, your subjects have inherited this freedom, that they should not be compelled to contribute to any tax, tallage, aid, or other like charge not set by common consent in Parliament:
Here we have the whole sophisticated apparatus of government moving into the operation of the collection of taxes on behalf of other authorities. We know what happened. Charles I levied a ship tax and eventually, in the argument, the Lords Temporal and Spiritual in the Commons won the battle and Charles I lost his head.
I think there might be a remedy for a situation such as this, namely, to have some provisional type of legislation. This was a point made by Mr. Coldwell, then the member for Rosetown-Biggar in the debate of 1948 on the famous amendment to the Excise Tax Act which caused some stir in that year. What I am trying to say in my participation in the debate is simply that I think it was a wrongful act for a department of government to set itself up to collect taxes for another level of governmental operation without any legislative sanction whatsoever. I do not think there is anything in the law now which would give the Department of National Revenue the right to take the course it has followed. I have made the point as best I can, and I would like to put the minister on notice that when the matter does go to the committee I expect that he, his parliamentary secretary or his senior officials, will have an answer to why this particular course is being followed.
As for the other points of the legislation, I have listened with great interest to the debate here. I would be concerned about the formula, particularly for university educational costs and about whether there is any possibility of getting some adjustment in the Blind Persons Act. I think that is important. They have been sending us petitions for years and it is time we gave these disabled persons a better break. However, Mr. Speaker, that can wait until the bill has received second reading and is studied in committee.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to thank you for affording me the opportunity of expressing my humble opinion on the bill now before us.
I have noted that the hon. member for Halifax-East Hants (Mr. McCleave) who has preceded me, has referred to "the so-called just society". I think he should not have used these words because, once uttered, they produce an adverse effect on the people in terms of the ideal which we are all pursuing, including the opposition parties. I believe that when the leader of the Liberal party spoke of the just society a few years ago, he was not promising to create a just society there and then.
I think that this slogan, or better still this motto, was proferred to the Canadian people as an aim which we should all strive to attain not only in the Liberal party and in the government, but all Canadians together. This is why I believe that the hon. member who spoke before me should not follow in the footsteps of others, and ridicule this slogan, at a time when we all need optimism, enthusiasm and motivation to direct our actions.
Mr. Speaker, my remarks will be limited to the two parts of the bill that interest me most and that I consider, in view of our needs, to be two most important, if not the most important part, that is Part I on equalization and Part VI on post-secondary education.
We can all discuss this problem and try to simplify it, but I think we all recognize the fact that it is a complex one and even the experts are not always successful in having us understand what actually is the meaning of equalization payments, of the transfers to the provinces in certain tax fields, and of all other aspects of the taxation problem.
Nevertheless, we all know this is a basic principle of Canada's Confederation. It is one of the corner-stores of Canadian unity and prosperity. It is not enough to say that Canada is a confederation of sovereign states. We must do more than that and I think the introduction of this bill we now have before is one step further in that direction.
It is not enough to say that Canada is a mosaic of ethnic groups; we must act accordingly and this is what we are doing.
510

March 3, 1972
Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements
There are people, even among foreigners, who will say that Canada is an artificial nation. Legislation such as the one before us help build this nation.
It may be true that Canada is an artificial nation but one must remember that this feature derives from men, that the artificial feature is a superior and transcendent natural feature.
I thinkT equalization is a means of saving our Confederation, of ensuring a decent standard of living for all Canadians and of allowing all of us to live together and avail ourselves of equal opportunities.
The equalization program is being critized by many. People in the Western provinces do criticize it, but I think that in my own province there are people who also object to it, perhaps not with words but with actior
Small groups in my province are trying to prove what little use it is for Quebec to be part of this group of peoples called Canada, and they overlook the equalization system which is designed to assist all the poor provinces which find it hard to keep up with the average level of public services in Canada, including Quebec.
I would like my fellow-citizens to remember the figures that have been quoted occasionally since the beginning of this debate. For instance, when we consider that in 195758 federal equalization payments granted to the provinces reached a total of $136 million and that they are expected to reach $1 billion in 1972-73 and $1.5 billion in 1976-77, we cannot help noticing the increase.
As for equalization payments, taking into consideration the percentages and the overall amounts given to certain provinces-Quebec being one of them-they may appear to be very high. If, however, we consider the per capita amount, we can then evaluate those figures more correctly. If we stop to think that Quebec's gross revenues for the year 1971-72 were roughly $2,764 million, as compared to Ontario's $4,291 million and Newfoundland's $168 million, we then realize that federal equalization payments do make sense.
This is why Quebec received, for the year 1971-72, federal equalization payments totalling $446 million, whereas Newfoundland received $110 million.
If we refer to the percentages of their own revenues, they are 65 per cent in the case of Newfoundland, and 16 per cent in the case of Quebec. Consequently, if a province such as Newfoundland had to levy taxes, for lack of those equalization payments, the income tax burden on the citizens of that province would be far too heavy.

What happens in countries which tend to drift into socialistic attitudes? We all recall the time a few years ago when certain Scandinavian countries, particularly Sweden, were held up to us as glowing examples of nations which had solved all their problems as far as business and people were concerned. We were told about the wonderful situation they had created for their citizens. This was a report on mental health and human environment written by Dr. Hans Lohman in Sweden. It describes what happens when people accept the premise that the state will look after people rather than people looking after people. I shall read some excerpts from this report as summarized in the newspaper.
The study points to a vicious circle in which a high rate of economic growth is necessary to pay the cost of looking after

those who cannot keep up, but as their number steadily increases a higher growth rate is needed, which only results in more people being unable to keep up-and so on.
The conclusion to be drawn from the report is that a country's welfare can no longer be measured simply by its standard of life, and that Swedes are increasingly sacrificing their mental health for improvements in their material environment.
This article then goes on to relate what is happening to countries that have tried to maintain this vast and all-encompassing social security program, and then says this about the rate of admissions for mental disorders in Sweden:
The latest available figures show that the number of inpatients admitted to mental institutions rose from 73,000 in 1969 to 83,000 in 1970-
This is costing the state $20 a day per patient, which means that over $1.5 million is being funnelled into keeping these patients under psychiatric care in mental institutions. The article continues:
A still greater number of out-patients were given light psychiatric care at public hospitals, while the enormous number who took to alcohol or drugs as a way out are not included in these statistics.
I read that only to show what is happening in countries in which the people depend on the state to too great an extent. Certainly, state welfare is not the paradise that some would lead us to believe.
To get back to the objections that I hear voiced by the people in the "have" provinces of Ontario, British Columbia and Alberta where the equalization payments originate, I may say that when industry is phased out the displaced workers have to be looked after. In many instances they do not want to move to a new community but rather wish to continue their lives in the same area. In this regard, I can think of no better example than workers in the Maritimes. I do not think workers made redundant should have to move to one of the "have" provinces. Indeed, I do not think the "have" provinces expect them to and, as a result, do not begrudge any payments they make under the equalization grants. But what does concern the "have" provinces is that with some families welfare is perpetuated from one generation to another. Families, for four or five generations, live off the largesse of government. This is a big problem and I do not have any easy answers to it. However, I do think that if a man remains unemployed during most of his life, some sort of manpower mobility program should be set up to see that the younger members of his family do move, perhaps to the "have" provinces where they will possibly be able to better themselves.
The subject or transportation has also been referred to in this debate. I agree with those who said that much of the money poured into equalization grants could very well be spent on equalizing transportation rates across Canada. Again with particular reference to the Maritimes, if the freight rates in the Maritimes were equalized with rates elsewhere, farmers in particular would have access to feed grains at the same price as those in the central provinces. They would be able to commence livestock feeding ventures or something of that kind which would enable them to help themselves. The same thing is true of industry. A transportation equalization program would

enable these people to help themselves to a far greater extent than is presently the case. Similarly, it would make industries more competitive and enable many other enterprises to break fresh ground, which at the moment they cannot afford to do.
The hon. member for Coast-Chilcotin (Mr. St. Pierre) who spoke prior to the lunch hour drew our attention to some figures relating to grants under the DREE program. He showed definitively the per capita ratios and pointed out that Alberta was third in the list of recipients of government funds under that program. Although I do not think anyone can argue with the figures that he presented, I do not believe he filled in the whole picture relating to grants. One of the major projects in Alberta that probably accounted for much of Alberta's share was the pulp mill at Grande Prairie. About $6 million was given to the Proctor and Gamble company, and I can only doubt the Wisdom of those who made this grant. We all know that pulp is presently at the stage of over-production in this country. Therefore, I see little point in giving $6 million to Proctor and Gamble and closing down another pulp mill in a different part of Canada. As I say, I question the judgment of those who made this decision.
Another complex in Alberta, which may be in the riding of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson), made an application to set up a hog factory that would produce over half a million hogs a year in the southern part of the province. I must say I can think of no more unlikely place in which to start a hog factory than southern Alberta. A better place would have been in the feed grain area of the province. One can only assume that there are certain political motives behind setting up a hog factory in that area. I also question whether, in view of over-production of hogs, we should have government competing with farmers.
Looking at Alberta in the total picture, I think if all factors were brought into account one would find that Alberta was in a far poorer position than many other provinces. Here again, I refer to the subject of freight rates. We in Alberta pay the freight on our products sent to Ontario and out to the west coast ports. In addition, we pay the producers in those areas for the freight to send their products back to us. In other words, we pay freight both ways. This was not revealed in the figures presented to the House by the hon. member for Coast-Chilcotin.
I can think of many other similar examples. There was a rapeseed processing plant contemplated not too many miles from where I lived which was regarded as a doubtful economic enterprise simply because of the cost of freight. Seed shipped out to the coast or to Ontario carries a freight subsidy. However, if the rapeseed is processed on the spot in Alberta, a different freight rate applies for the end product. On the other hand, anyone who builds a processing plant in Ontario can have the rapeseed shipped to him at the subsidized freight rate. Such a person is in a much better position and more likely to have a profitable operation. These are the things which work against the provinces that are not in central Canada.
I shall not continue much further, Mr. Speaker, but I wish to stress that there is ample evidence to indicate that

the whole matter of regional incentives needs review. I cannot see that we are getting the desired results in many of the areas that are the prime recipients of these transfers of money. The people in those provinces which contribute to these funds have a right to an accounting from the federal government on how the funds are being spent. It is true that the federal government can generalize when asked how the funds are being spent, but it should indicate more specifically what the success ratio has been. Funds are being pumped into these areas in ever increasing amounts. The federal government will find itself in a position of great difficulty if any attitude of rebellion appears in some of the contributing provinces, from whose coffers money is taken. This may happen if the federal government does not show more responsibility for the performance achieved from the expenditure of this money.

I was born and brought up in the province of Saskatchewan, and I lived the active years of my youth there during the great depression. Like a lot of other people who were young at that time and going to university, the most important event of the day to me was the great imquest conducted into our national affairs by the Rowell Sirois Commission and the publication of its report on Dominion-Provincial relations in 1940. Certainly, at that time in western Canada it appeared as if the terms of confederation had been switched inside out. We were suffering from a great depression, from drought and other factors which made life in Saskatchewan very difficult and reduced the income of the province to minimal proportions. speechtext:
The hon. member for Cape Breton says central Canada. But more than that, the head offices of most of the business and financial institutions were in central Canada. In those days we used to speak a lot about the evils of Bay Street and St. James Street, two well known thoroughfares in the cities of Toronto and Montreal. But all through the discussion there was a realization that it was impossible in a country like ours to equalize every economic opportunity, to equalize access to every source of personal or business income. It was quite apparent then, and I think it is still apparent that different parts of this country at different times will achieve differential benefits from confederation. For example, in those days the province of Alberta was almost as badly off as the province of Saskatchewan. It was most definitely a "have-not" province. It is now, as we have just been told by the hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Downey), a have province. I hope this does not change, but these are casual circumstances which can and do change, as our history shows.
March 3, 1972

What is important is how we respond to the challenge of this basic situation, to the changes that occur, so that at all times in this country there will be some basic equity and equality in the provision of governmental services for our citizens. As hon. members know, from the very beginning of our history there has been continual fighting about the financial terms. The ink was hardly dry on the British North America Act before the cry came up from the distinguished province of Nova Scotia for better terms. In one way or another ever since there has been a claim by one province or another, by one section of Canada or another, for better terms.
As the great report of the Rowell-Sirois Commission pointed out, for many years it was possible for these pressures to be adjusted on a more or less casual political basis. In the early years of this century, the role of government in our affairs was nowhere nearly as great as it is now, and it was possible to make adjustments which were essentially ad hoc, which from time to time quelled the clamour of different parts of Canada. However, this whole operation came apart during the depression. The gimmickry, the jerrybuilt structure of federal-provincial financial relations could not stand the test of the depression which put ever increasing pressures on governments for increased expenditures.
This fact was recognized by the Rowell-Sirois report, and I think it might be appropriate at this time to quote a portion from its main recommendations, Book II, page 269 giving the analysis of this great commission of the essential problem of our confederation. I quote At the heart of the problem lie the needs of Canadian citizens. These needs, whether material or cultural, can be satisfied only if all the provincial governments in Canada are in a position to supply those services which the citizen of today demands of them. The ability of provincial governments to meet the demands of their citizens depends in part on the constitutional powers which they enjoy, in part on their financial capacity to perform their recognized functions. The striking fact in the Commission's study of Canadian conditions is that many provinces, whose financial position is not the result of emergency conditions, are unable to find the money to enable them to meet the needs of their citizens. The basic problem before the Commission lies, therefore, in finding a way in which the financial position of the provinces could be improved and assured, without disastrous financial consequences to the Federal Government on whose efficient functioning all provinces are dependent. National unity and provincial autonomy must not be thought of as competitors for the citizen's allegiance for, in Canada at least, they are but two facets of the same thing- a sane federal system. National unity must be based on provincial autonomy, and provincial autonomy cannot be assured unless a strong feeling of national unity exists throughout Canada.
As hon. members are well aware, arguing from that strong premise the royal commission recommended the elimination of all the ancient deals which had been made between the federal government and the provinces, and between the provinces, to hold the financial structure together. It recommended what we have seen develop since the war, a system of payments from the federal treasury which will ensure to people in all parts of Canada a basic common level of governmental services.
At another stage in this report, in commenting upon this recommendation in more detail the Royal Commission had the following to say at page 274, also in Book II:
... the Dominion was to pay subsidies in 1867 to enable the
Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements
provinces to perform the functions entrusted to them without having to resort to oppressive taxation. Under the Commission's proposals the Dominion would pay National Adjustment Grants for precisely the same purpose. It is true that a different measure of the amount to be paid to each province would be adopted now than that which was then considered appropriate. But this difference is more apparent than real, for it arises from the inequalities of wealth which have developed as between the provinces. Equal per capita subsidies did conform in some rough approximation to the fiscal needs of 1867. They would not do so today. The Commission hopes that the method which it has employed for calculating the appropriate adjustment grants will be able to accomplish what the per capita formula was intended to achieve in 1867, for, though the means have changed, the end remains the same, namely the maintenance of provincial governments which can provide the necessary services for their people.
What I have quoted illustrates the truth that everyone here in this House would recognize, namely that nothing has changed in our confederation since its commencement. There was then a recognized need for the federal government to contribute to the revenue of different provinces so as to enable them to provide services for their people. That need has continued down through all the 100 or more years. It continues today, and it is the responsibility of this parliament to respond to that need and to provide legislation and measures which are appropriate for satisfying them.
The hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Downey) who preceded me made a comment which I think must be noted. He said, in effect, that there are taxpayers in some provinces who are paying the shot for other provinces, that the good citizens of Alberta are picking up the fiscal tab for the people of Nova Scotia. Whatever the situation may be in his mind, it is different in reality; it is different so far as confederation and the life of this nation are concerned. There are taxpayers all over this country paying taxes to the federal government, and perhaps most of them feel they are too high.
