The talk in this Chamber about the level of taxes is always very interesting, but the real question is how will the taxes be disposed of by the governments which receive them. It is to this question that I will direct my attention. The suggestion is made that somehow or other we who are taxpayers in Ontario, those people who are taxpayers in Alberta and those who are taxpayers in British Columbia, are paying their money directly to other provinces such as Newfoundland, Prince Edward Island, Quebec, or any of the other provinces, and that there is something illegitimate and improper in that. There is the suggestion that because we live in the three provinces I have mentioned we have some kind of super role of surveillance which providence has cast upon us in respect of the expenditures made by other provinces which receive some of these grants.
I think that it is well at this stage to look in totality at what takes place in this country in terms of all the grants

March 3, 1972
Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements and all the payments which are made by the federal government to all the provinces of Canada. I refer to a document which was published by the Treasury Board entitled "How your Tax Dollar is Spent, 1972-73" and more particularly to page 31 where a table is set forth showing the estimated federal payments to provinces and municipalities for the coming fiscal year. The totals disclosed in these tables are themselves impressive. In all, when allowance is made for tax abatements, the total amount of federal funds which is payable to the provinces is $5,205 million, which is approximately one third of the total estimates of the federal government for the coming year which are stated to be $15,700 million.
But let us look at how some of these funds are distributed. For example, the total of all federal payments to the province of Quebec is $1,665 million, the total for Ontario is $1,423 million. The next highest province is British Columbia where the total is $360 million. The next highest province is Alberta where the total is $316.5 million, and so on. It is true that some provinces do not receive equalization payments, but the equalization payments for the current year are estimated to be $944 million out of a total of all federal grants to all provinces for all purposes of $5.2 billion.
So, I suggest that we should look at federal expenditures in their total perspective and realize that the responsibilities which this government and parliament have assumed spread across a broad spectrum of our country. They cover all kinds of services to people in all provinces, and it is quite improper, unjust and unfair for some politicians in some provinces to suggest that they are carrying a load when large amounts of money, for example, are paid to the Atlantic provinces, to some of the western provinces, and to the province of Quebec. It is also unfair for anyone to suggest that there is some kind of impropriety, as Premier Bennett has suggested, in the calculation of these payments, that somehow or other the provinces in eastern Canada do not have to account properly for all their revenues in the determination of revenue potentials when in fact they do.
I have spoken here simply to suggest that there are good reasons for carrying on with this system of tax equalization. It is something which we have had throughout the whole history of our country. It is something which has been applied in an increasingly rational and sensible fashion since the report of the Rowell-Sirois Royal Commission in 1940. If we are going to maintain not only the unity of this country but decent standards of life in all parts of Canada, then it will be necessary for us to overcome the infirmities of economics in different provinces and jurisdictional problems by continuing to pay equalization payments. Therefore, I support the legislation which has been put before us.

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS ACT. AUTHORIZATION OF FISCAL PAYMENTS TO AND TAX COLLECTION AGREEMENTS WITH PROVINCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to speak to the bill under consideration.
I wish to say what I think about the equalization payments and the situation in which the government finds itself with regard to the provinces in that respect.

Mr. Speaker, the federal budget is close to $16 billion. Transfer payments to provinces, including tax exemptions, will total $5.2 billion during the next fiscal year, that is one third of the budgetary commitments of the central government. However, the funds needed for the administration of the Old Age Security Fund and for advances and loans eventually repayable are not included.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, the budgets of the provinces add up to about the same as that of Ottawa. In general, the provinces therefore get one third of their money from the federal treasury.
Such a policy is inadequate. Is it realistic? It is therefore not surprising, Mr. Speaker, in those circumstances, that the provinces feel that they are not receiving enough from the federal government.
Seven provinces receive tax rebates from the central government. And all of them are not satisfied, and feel that they are not getting enough, and, even Quebec and the three other provinces that receive nothing are not satisfied. They state that the central government is asking too much of them, and that it is not logical to be so highly taxed, because those provinces, that are said to be rich, are those in need of revenue, as they do not have enough. The citizens of the latter provinces, like those of the others, have to pay close to 50 per cent of their income.
According to some economists, we are now paying 50 per cent of our income to provincial, federal and municipal governments and to school boards. Taxpayers say that they are not satisfied and that they are unable to make ends meet. They claim that they will be unable to put up with this very long, that it is impossible that taxes should be further increased when they are already paying 50 per cent of their income in taxes.
In the case of Quebec, equalization payments amount to $446 million, that is 10 per cent of the provincial budget. Conditional payments, hospital insurance, the Canada Assistance Plan, health insurance will bring in a contribution of $440 million, that is 20 per cent of the budget.
Mr. Bourassa's last estimates totalled $4.5 billion. Now, for the coming fiscal year Quebec will receive from the federal government grants of $1.5 billion, that is one third of its budget. If to this are added the tax rebates arbitrarily set by the federal government, the direct or indirect amounts handed to Quebec by Ottawa represent $1.6 billion.
Now, under the circumstances, can the provinces, even in their own fields, talk on an equal footing with Ottawa, when the two levels of government have to share sources of revenue.
Federal-provincial conferences have been held for several years, but they have failed to satisfy the provincial as well as the federal government. Canada has therefore reached a very high degree of federal-provincial tax coordination. We have developped an elaborate and efficient procedure to increase provincial revenues.
For the next financial year, Mr. Speaker, Newfoundland will receive $213 per capita; Prince Edward Island, $214; New Brunswick, $164; Nova Scotia, $135; Saskatchewan, $102; Manitoba, $59 and Quebec, $74.
March 3, 1972

I would not hesitate to say that the present taxation system is vitiated just as the financial system is. It is contrary to the hard economic realities. It is used for centralization in the hands of the financial empire of the state.
Modern taxation is illegal, even though it is effected through a political democracy which, for its participation, gets an insignificant share of its advantages. I think that it is rather the pursuit of an objective which can be nothing but socialism. Economists trained at the London School of Economics claimed that it is possible to reach happiness by condoning the theft of property through taxes.
Present financing and taxation are but means of concentration of financial power. It is obvious that taxation, under its present form, is an inefficient and irritating way of achieving the desired objective. Be that as it may, some form of taxation is inevitable as long as public services and production to meet private needs co-exist.
Public services demand a minimum of goods and labour; the mechanism through which those goods and labour are transferred from the private to the public sector is essentially a form of taxation.
Some claim that through equalization payments, the people can provide both private and public goods. But under the present system, goods are taken away from people who do not have enough, for private production, under the pretext of allowing public production. But in other cases, taxes are in essences legalized robbery. For instance, when taxes take away the purchasing power of the individuals, while production waits for buyers.
The government is levying taxes for functions that should be left to individuals, families and intermediary bodies. The robbery increases as government interference is stepped up. It is true that the government always alleges the financial inability of persons, families and public bodies, when it should apply itself to removing this inability, as a financial system working for the public good would do.
I say that taxes are a nonsense, because the collection is too costly and it is the taxpayer who has to pay for it all without getting anything in return. Under a system consistent with reality we would not have to levy taxes to meet the ever growing financial needs of the social insurance services. As co-heirs and co-proprietors of the capital the citizens should find a unconditional economic security in the guaranteed social income accompanied by an adjustment of the prices, because all physical possibilities would simply become financial possibilities. The public would be able to pay for all the production originating in the private sector of the economy. Thus the public service expenses would not be, as they are today, a burden or a hindrance to the obtainment of goods from the private sector.
On the other hand, a guaranteed income for everyone, at least for the basic necessaries of life, would ensure a fair amount of well-being, according to our productive capacity.
To have a correct perspective of the civilized world, one must be realist. The standard of living would no longer
Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements depend on the financial system, but on actual or potential production. Finance would intervene only to lubricate the machinery of production and to protect the freedom of the consumer.
Government measures should be geared to the financing and development of our physical potential.
Mr. Speaker, if we must always, in order to meet requirements of provinces and claims of the poorer ones, do what we accomplished with Bill C-259, the government will tax citizens to the point of empoverishing them, of wiping them out. Mr. Speaker, since so many provinces are poor, since they have so many problems, we must improve their system in order to keep them afloat, to enable them to develop their public schools and institutions, in short to enable them to keep pace reasonably with science and progress. We could certainly help the provinces, so long as men are willing to work and the plough is tilling the earth.
Mr. Speaker, so long as the earth will be supplying more than the total population requirements, we should feel no insecurity. Yet, all the provinces are now insecure, wondering how to balance their budgets, meet interest payments on our debts to financial institutions.

And we can still go further if we make available to the people all possible financial controls to achieve that growth. But as long as we give only crumbs to the provinces, as long as we tax people to the extreme to prevent them from living decently, we will have difficulties at the provincial level, we will experience the threat of separatism and revolution because of the inefficiency of the government in giving people what they are entitled to. As long as we stay as we are, there will be credit restrictions, dissatisfied provinces, revolutions, because the people are unable to provide for their needs and because the financial economic system does not meet with people's requirements.
We know that all provinces would like to do more for the people and give more to them. Schools are now being built in all provinces with borrowed money at 8 or 9 per cent rates of interest. All those provinces will have to repay those loans in 10 years and the interest will be doubled by that time. We shall have paid for such schools or institutions in 20 years twice their value, in 30 years thrice, and in 40 years four times.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to add a few remarks to this debate. I promise the House they will be few. I do hot want to let the opportunity go by without expressing a point of view directed particularly to post-secondary education and the way in which the present formula affects, adversely in my view, institutions of higher learning in the Atlantic provinces.
I agree with the opening statement of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) that there is probably no other piece of legislation, no matter how dry it sounds and no matter how dull the debate, which affects the federal state more than the bill dealing with equalization payments to various provinces.
Having been born and raised in one of the so-called have-not provinces, Nova Scotia, and having contributed, I suppose in a small way, to the gross national product in one of the "have" provinces, British Columbia, I feel that though I am by no means an expert, my experience as a professional man in the community as well as my experience as a politician permits me to say that we are all part of the family of Canada. As in any family, there are various contributors to the home. Their age differs, as does their state of health. When a family is seated around a supper table, the mother and the father are normally present. In the case of Canada, I suppose one could say that the mother and the father are the two central provinces of Ontario and Quebec. These are certainlv the two founding provinces.
Then there are the other provinces, some, in the west, expanding because of their basic economic wealth and others, in the east, going through a transitional period, not sharing in the growth rate of other parts of the country. To reduce this question to a common denominator one ought to consider equalization in the light of a family sitting around a table. The provinces of Canada make up, in their various jurisdictions, the family of Canada. The smallest and weakest member of the family has a part to play, just as do the big brothers and the older sisters. So I am in complete agreement with the Minister of Finance when he said that this equalization concept is the cornerstone of the federal system. In fact, I would go further and

say it is the foundation of the federal system-because if there is no equalization within the economy, that is, within the family, what is left?
I should like to compliment the Minister of Finance on his new and challenging post. It so happens, I suppose because of the legislative platter before the House last session, that he had to introduce an equalization bill as his first item of business. There is no item that he could have introduced more important to the federal system in Canada, not just important to us in the east but to the west and the central provinces as well. After all, the whole is only as strong as the parts, and the parts make up the whole.
I come back to my analogy of the family. The squalling, squealing baby in the crib, with which the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) is confronted when he goes home from a busy day in this House, has something to contribute to the household, the same as the older brother or sister and the two parents. We all have our part to play: the equalization concept recognizes this fact.
Since, hopefully, we shall conclude this debate this afternoon, I will make my remarks brief. I should like to philosophize further on the concept of the "have" provinces contributing to the have-not provinces. That in itself is a myth, because for the "have" provinces to develop the wherewithal or money to contribute to the have-not provinces they have to be part of the whole. People in Ontario and Quebec are able to produce certain tax revenues because they have been able to benefit from various policies that helped other regions.
We now have British Columbia, developing and economically booming, able to contribute to other provinces. Many years ago, years which many people want to forget about or have forgotten about, B.C. was given a form of equalization grant when Canadian taxpayers subsidized and in effect helped to build the Canadian Pacific railway to bring together the country from coast to coast. The railway certainly was not built to carry passengers or freight to the sparsely populated and remote parts of the country at that time. Nevertheless, out of a concept that did not start with the present government or the previous one but goes back more than 60 years, British Columbia has grown buoyant and rich. I myself participated in their economy in a small way for seven years. British Columbia is now a "have" province and can help the rest of Canada in the sense of developing its raw materials and other resources in the province.
I should like to comment on one thing that the Minister of Finance said in regard to the three concepts that the Rowell-Sirois commission defined for Canada in his maiden address as Minister of Finance in opening this debate on March 1. This commission, which was fundamental really to the future of Canada, wrote that the federal authorities were to develop a financial role so that there would be national growth and stability; secondly, fair standards in public services and, thirdly, co-ordination in tax policy.
I could have much to say about tne present government, the former minister of finance, the hon. member for Kingston (Mr. Benson), and the tax reform bill. They have
March 3, 1972

fallen flat on their faces in regard to co-ordinating federal tax policy with tax policy at the provincial and municipal levels, so much so that unless measures are taken by this new Minister of Finance we will recreate the tax jungle that we had in Canada prior to the Rowell-Sirois commission. I hope the minister will show some new life, energy and initiative so that we once again do not get into this morass of financial swampland.
Coming particularly to the post-secondary education part of the equalization bill, namely part VI, which in effect extends post-secondary payments for another two years, with a ceiling of up to 15 per cent of the national average, I want to mention several areas of concern. Firstly, of course, in Atlantic Canada there is fundamental concern that the formula for post-secondary education was changed in 1966 in order to get away from a per capita student cost basis to a 50 per cent shared cost basis vis-a-vis operating expenses.
The Secretary of State (Mr. Pelletier), who is responsible for this part of the program, quite correctly says that mushrooming post-secondary education costs have risen more than the educator pot, increasing from $422 million in 1967-68 to $870 million for 1971-72. In Atlantic Canada we have, historically, educated Canadians from many parts of the country. I come basically from what is a poor province. However, in many ways we were better off with a per capita payment for our students, especially students from Ontario, Quebec and other provinces in Canada, than we are under the present program where we receive from the federal treasury 50 per cent of our operating costs.
Very simply and fundamentally, in the province I come from, Nova Scotia-the picture is the same in the other Atlantic provinces-we cannot develop the level of help for post-secondary education that other provinces can. Sharing on a 50-50 basis the operating expenditure, since the 50 per cent from the provincial treasury is a relatively low figure in view of the realities of provincial financing in Nova Scotia and Atlantic Canada in general, obviously the 50 per cent we receive from the federal treasury is also low. Yet we still have a large influx of students from other parts of the country. One of the things we can do in Atlantic Canada is build educational institutions. Historically, we have been the provider of education for many who have gone elsewhere in Canada in fields of business, science, politics and the church.

We have seen the same kind of prejudice in my own province of British Columbia. It has been said in that province that the principle of equalization is wrong and, by illustration, that Quebec gets too much. Mr. Speaker, if there are those who oppose equalization, let them say that. If there are those who oppose the French language in Canada, let them say that. But let them not confuse and divide by mixing the two together.
If politicians in British Columbia oppose equalization grants only, then why do they always use Quebec as an illustration of why they are wrong? After all, Quebec, with grants of $74 per capita, is the second lowest of all the receiving provinces. If there is any conflict or any complaint why not talk about Newfoundland, with $213 per capita, or New Brunswick, the home province of the Premier of British Columbia, with $164 per capita?
I can only assume that what is meant by British Columbia politicians is that it is only wrong to have equalization grants for French-speaking provinces and it is all right to have them for English-speaking provinces. If there is any complaint from British Columbia, surely it should be with regard to Prince Edward Island, which gets two-thirds of its revenues from equalization grants. It is not my purpose to complain about Prince Edward Island.
The reasons for this apparent anomaly are part of our constitutional heritage, as are certain of our French-language rights which also are part of our heritage. My objection is not with Prince Edward Island; it is not with Quebec. It is not with any province. Rather, it is a complaint against those who create such issues for the purpose of building their own power.
There was never a better example of the old adage of divide and rule than the present course of action being followed by a few provincial politicians in British Columbia. There have been suggestions that British Columbia would challenge equalization rights in the courts. Where is that challenge? It has disappeared. It has disappeared in the laughter of constitutional experts in Canada.
There have been other foolish things recently said by some British Columbia politicians. There have been claims that wages are especially low in Quebec and that this is why equalization grants are unfair. Again, why single out Quebec? Wages are low in Quebec, but they are lower in Newfoundland, Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick. I could go on, Mr. Speaker.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) dealt with a number of these items the other day when he spoke on the same subject and demolished many similar arguments. In the time remaining I wish to make only a few remarks. Canada is a big nation, a family of provinces, a federalism. Any family has to learn to live together. A family with no strains, no tensions, is a family without deep or developing relations. As a British Columbian I support the principle of equalization grants and I assure the House that most British Columbians feel the same way 
and are equally strong in support of any necessary measures for maintaining a strong federalism and a strong ten provinces in Canada.

Earlier today I referred to a press report relating to an incident which occurred yesterday when Mr. Roger Jay, secretary of the Union of Ontario Indians, sought to deliver a press release to the House of Commons press gallery. Inquiries into this incident confirm that Mr. Jay presented himself at the main entrance of the centre block of the Parliament buildings for the purpose of delivering a press release. The normal practice would have
March 3, 1972

been for the desk sergeant to communicate with the press gallery to arrange either for the delivery of the papers to the Canadian Press representative in the gallery or for the press officer to have the parcel picked up at the desk. Instead, Mr. Jay was directed to the office of the chief of the protective service where, after conversations, contact was established with Mr. Mollins of the Canadian Press.
The chief of the protective staff of the House of Commons gives the assurance that the action taken was not inspired by the contents of the release but only to ensure that the papers were indeed intended for distribution to the press gallery. At the same time, it would appear that the procedure adopted by the security personnel was irregular and that it did cause Mr. Jay inconvenience and embarrassment.
In the circumstances, I have no hesitation in saying on behalf of all hon. members that the incident is a regrettable one, and express the hope that such incidents can be avoided in the future.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED INCREASE IN EXEMPTION LEVELS TO COUNTERACT INCREASED COST OF LIVING
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of introducing legislative measures so that the income of Canadians will be adjusted to the increasing cost of living by eliminating all taxes for single persons earning less than $3,000 and for married couples earning less than $5,000 with the addition of a further $500 exemption for each dependent child.
Mr. Speaker, the reason I am presenting a motion today is that I am convinced that the adjustments made at the
Income Tax Exemptions
time the tax reform bill was passed last fall, or rather at the end of last year, are clearly inadequate.
In spite of all the talk which has been going on these past few years about the establishment of the just society, I fail to see any real justice in a small exemption of $1,500 for single people and $2,850 for married couples. I think it is somewhat ridiculous to levy taxes at this level. If we compare, for instance, these amounts with the governor general's salary of $46,500 a year and take into account the fact that this same person who lives among us enjoys a $72,000 a year expense account for entertainment, gifts, medal awards, and government house administration, that is to pay the salaries of kitchen and household staff and all the retinue around him, this situation cannot be justified.
Canadians are well aware that they are being double-crossed by this government. It is true that this administration has published a white paper on taxation so that Canadians could argue their case, but this procedure is to me only a bluff, since the amendments to Bill C-259 have exclusively favoured large associations and corporations. The voice of small earners has not been heard and when some labour associations or citizens made representations, it was obvious that they were ignored because they could not contribute to the electoral fund of the old parties. I think that this is why no amendment was tabled in favour of the working class.
I must recognize, for example, that following the reaction of those who could contribute to electoral funds, the government has been prepared to introduce some amendments.
Mr. Speaker, if we consider that 70 per cent of the country's revenues are paid up by those earning less than $5,000 a year, then there is cause for concern. What is to me a flagrant injustice is evidenced by the comparison between the taxes levied on workers and those paid by oil companies. When one considers that from 1965 to 1968, oil companies have paid only $45 million in taxes, that is 5.7 per cent on profits amounting to $795 million, then there is other cause for concern.
Mr. Speaker, the motion I am introducing today for tax exemption for all single people earning under $3,000 per annum and married couples earning under $5,000 per annum, is based on the fact that they are always and everywhere considered as taxpayers. At all government levels, they pay the same price as anybody else. Nothing, be it municipal taxes, school taxes or insurance services, can be paid by them at reduced prices. If they are lucky enough to get a $3,000 car, for instance, they have to pay the 12 per cent federal tax and, if in Quebec, the 8 per cent provincial tax, as anybody else. If they wish to get a 40-ounce bottle of whisky, they have to pay the same price as anybody else-$8.75.
In that connection, Mr. Speaker, it is quite enlightening to consider who are the end recipients of the amount of $8.75 paid by the consumer for the 40-ounce bottle of Canadian whisky since we know that the distiller sells it for $1.22 only.
First of all, the federal government takes 44 cents for sales tax, and $2.49 for excise tax. The provincial government's share in Quebec amounts to $3.94. This already

March 3, 1972
Income Tax Exemptions
makes $8.10 per bottle. If one adds the 8 per cent provincial tax, one reaches the figure of $8.75.
It is worth noting that 10 years ago the consumer paid $6.90; since then, the distiller's share has increased by only 22 cents; the balance, that is $1.63, is being divided between the federal government and the provincial government.
Now, why should people be surprised to find out that some of them have one glass too many and develop stomach ulcers. No wonder since they end up drinking a much larger quantity of taxes than of liquids. Sooner or later, they wake up with a hangover and related injuries.
Mr. Speaker, whether the worker is earning $4,000 or $10,000 a year, the price for gas is the same, about 50 cents a gallon. Of this amount, the federal government collects about 4 cents while the province of Quebec, for instance, gets 19 cents.
We know that this also applies to a 30-cent loaf of bread. The western wheat producer, the miller who prepared the flour, the baker, the wholesale dealer, the retailer and all those who worked hard and who have been living on fractions of cents in profit could sell us their bread for 15 cents if it were not for all the taxes they have had to pay at all levels of government.
Studies have proven that there were 100 indirect taxes on bread. It is astonishing to see how little taxpayers realize the total amount of taxes they are paying each year.
For instance, at the retail level, the humiliating feature of the sales tax is obvious. If you add up the aggregate amount of taxes paid by a family over one year you reach an astonishing amount. Moreover, most consumers completely forget that the prices imposed by the manufacturers must necessarily include their own taxes.
With the present system, it is unavoidable and unfortunate that the lower income people have to pay a major portion of the revenue required by the governments for their services and programs.
The corporate tax is another kind of indirect tax imposed without the taxpayer's knowledge. This burden compels corporations to reduce their dividends; in fact their benefits are now so low that the shareholders seem to be under maximum pressure. The only way out for a corporation is to increase its sales price. Mr. Speaker, taxes do amount to a theft when imposed on taxpayers who do not have enough money to get the things they need to live at a time when there is an abundance of goods in Canada.
Taxes also amount to a theft so long as there are unsold products, unemployment and an undeveloped capacity of production because of a lack of purchasing power which in turn stymies the sale of goods.
Taxes amount to a theft at a time like this because they limit the purchasing power, lead to an accumulation of products and deprive the people in the same way as inflation does. In fact, taxes should exist only to absorb the money surplus in circulation at the very time when there is a shortage of products. When there is no money, we do not need taxes but an increased purchasing power.

From the start, we have to recognize that every direct or indirect tax leads to an increase in the prices of goods and services. It is always the consumer who pays the bill. The real taxpayer is always the consumer.
An eminent professor gave a lecture which appeared in Le Devoir on May 31, 1971 and in which he suggested that Ottawa should reduce income tax for individuals and sales tax. He said in part:
The government should reduce the income tax of individuals and the federal sales tax in order to stimulate productivity and slow down salary inflation, said economist Grant L. Reuber, director of the Department of Economics at Western University, in London.
Professor Reuber, a former president of the Canadian Economics Association, submitted to the Senate Committee on Finance some suggestions that are contrary to federal theories on the management of the economy.
In an oral and written submission that he presented in collaboration with economist Ronald G. Bodkin, Mr. Reuber questioned the arguments put forward by Prime Minister Pierre Elliott Trudeau, Finance Minister E. J. Benson and Prices and Incomes Commission Chairman John Young against tax cuts.
According to Mr. Reuber, the Bank of Canada has intensified the economic problems of Canada by going from one extreme to the other and by alternating the limitations on credit and the influx of capital in the banking system.
Mr. Reuber has agreed that the economy is moving ahead after the recession of 1970, but unemployment will not go down much below 5 per cent of the labour force. It now stands at about 6 per cent.
That is why the government should pursue a "moderately expansionary tax policy", promote expenses likely to stimulate the demand for goods and services, in order to multiply employment.
Mr. Speaker, we are witnessing an opposite phenomenon, for never have the burdens of the worker been so heavy. And still more surprising, is that each year, the taxpayers are called to pay increasingly higher taxes under the item of the public debt and incurred interests.
In 1969-70, actual expenditures under the public debt amounted to $1,709,938,172. In 1970-71, those expenditures amounted to $1,862,400,000 and finally for 1971-72, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) then anticipated a public debt expenditure for the tidy sum of $1,988 million.
Mr. Speaker, if we take into account the fact that Canada has some 21 million inhabitants and that the interests to be paid amount to $1,988 million, this represents something like $100 per year for each Canadian citizen.
Now, one should recall that, after the Second World War, the per capita interest on the national debt was $26.42 and that, in 1960, it was $42.17. Twelve years later, that is in 1972, every Canadian will have to pay $100 for this. Such are the fruits of the financial system that current and previous governments have favoured and continue to favour.
Some will no doubt say that that is a good thing and, unfortunately, they are the ones who represent high finance.
If we investigated, we would find that those to whom the interest on the public debt is paid and who will receive the $2 billion or so that Canadians will pay in 1972 are not people who earn only a pittance.
March 3, 1972

On the contrary, they are in the higher tax brackets and a major part of this interest just goes to swell bankers' dividends.
Mr. Speaker, since in view of all kinds of tax increases the national debt is still rising, we arrive at the conclusion that taxes paid by small wage-earners are just money wasted which, ultimately, serves only to swell the wealth of high finance.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has already asked the working population of the country to tighten their belts. The constant increase of the cost of the debt in interest charges makes it clear that this appeal was meant for high finance.
Mr. Speaker, that is why I am now offering this government an opportunity to demonstrate fairness in establishing its budget by curtailing the amounts allocated to the national debt and, as a result, to evolve a tax system to relieve single people earning less than $3,000 a year and married people earning less than $5,000 a year.

subtopic: INCOME TAX
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED INCREASE IN EXEMPTION LEVELS TO COUNTERACT INCREASED COST OF LIVING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in speaking on the motion of the hon. member for Portneuf (Mr. Godin), I would congratulate him for bringing the motion before the House. It is a very important one. When we talk about basic exemptions for income tax, if we look far enough ahead we can see that no matter what is proposed, the chances are that it will come to pass some time in the future. So it is well that we should seriously consider this matter this afternoon.
I am pleased, too, that the hon. member has been able to enlighten us on some of the Social Credit theories and the benefits thereof. I am very sorry that these things have never come to pass in the provinces of Alberta and British Columbia which have had the wisdom to support Social Credit. However, Mr. Speaker, that does not in any way detract from the importance of this motion.
The hon. member for Portneuf has suggested that the amendments passed during the last 12 months did not go far enough in providing basic exemptions. I think this amendment is always true, but it is a case of trying to balance equity against growth in the economy.
It seems to me that in the two or three years when we debated the white paper on tax reform, and especially in 1969, we were enjoying rapid growth. Young people had not entered the work force in such large numbers and unemployment was at a lower level than it has been recently. Of course, as time went on-and this has been most evident in the past 12 months-it seems to me people felt that we should adopt a tax system and introduce budgets that would provide for growth in the economy. Certainly the warnings of the Economic Council of Canada bore out what would happen if that were not done. The council in its projection contended that we needed something like 6 per cent of real growth in the economy for the next four or five years.
I think we have been pretty successful in reaching this growth level. In 1971 real growth in our economy was at the 6 per cent rate. Our rate of growth between 1968 and 1971 averaged pretty nearly that figure. The Economic
Income Tax Exemptions
Council of Canada has told us that 1.4 million new jobs must be created between now and 1975. If this rate of growth is maintained we will be able to absorb into the work force many of the 1.4 additional people who will be entering the work force.
As the debate on tax policy developed, it became clear that people wanted a more equitable tax system and that we should strive to introduce a progressive tax system in which the person earning more pays more. We must also recognize that we want the economy to grow if we are to provide jobs for people entering the work force. If you are not working and are not earning any income, it really does not matter to you how high the basic exemption levels are. However, being against this motion would be like being against motherhood. We all know how difficult it is for a single person to get along on less than $3,000 a year, or for a married couple to get along on less than $5,000, the amounts set out in the notice of motion.
The hon. member also talked about the inequity of the sales tax. During the debate on the tax reform bill last fall the former minister of finance indicated that in the years ahead we would be reviewing taxes and reconsidering the sales tax. I agree with this. The hon. member for Portneuf used the example of sales tax on a bottle of whisky. I did not think that example was appropriate. If he had chosen bread, meat or something like that, his example might have been more appropriate. The sales tax is a flat tax; it taxes the poor and the rich alike at the same rate. The genius and beauty of the income tax is that it taxes progressively: a person who makes more pays more.
The notice of motion before the House reads:
That in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of introducing legislative measures so that the income of Canadians will be adjusted to the increasing cost of living by eliminating all taxes for single persons earning less than $3,000 and for married couples earning less than $5,000 with the addition of a further $500 exemption for each dependent child.
The notice of motion uses the words, "by eliminating all taxes for single persons earning less than $3,000 and for married couples earning less than $5,000". It also refers to a further $500 exemption for each dependent child. The proposal to eliminate tax for those earning under $3,000 or $5,000 could be accomplished by starting points or exemptions. The starting point device is used by the province of Quebec which provides that an individual does not pay income tax unless his income exceeds $2,000 if single and $4,000 if married. When an individual's income exceeds these amounts, the basic exemptions of $1,500 and $2,850 come into play. Thus, if a single individual has an income of, say, $2,001, he would become taxable on $501, the amount permitted by the federal exemption. However, this is prevented by a notch provision which has been introduced to prevent the tax reducing income below the starting points.
On the other hand, an exemption of a stated amount applies to everyone. For example, an exemption of $3,000 for single persons would eliminate from the tax rolls everyone with income of less than this amount and would also permit all single taxpayers to deduct $3,000 from income in computing taxable income. The advantage of the starting point device is that it is much less costly in terms of revenue. However, it requires a notch provision for income that is just above the starting points. Even

March 3, 1972
Income Tax Exemptions
with such a provision the marginal rate on such income is likely to be very high.
No matter whether the hon. member has in mind starting points or exemptions at the $3,000 and $5,000 levels, the government's position might be that this matter was extensively reviewed following the report of the Royal Commission on Taxation, the preparation of the white paper on tax reform and the preparation of the tax reform income tax amendments passed by Parliament in December, 1971. There was considerable debate in the House on this subject when the white paper was discussed and during consideration of Bill C-259 last session. The exemptions recommended by the government and accepted by Parliament in the legislation passed in December, 1971, apply for 1972 and subsequent years and are as follows: for a person of single status, $1,500; for a person of married status, $2,850; for a dependent under 16, $300, and for a dependent over 16, $550-or $50 more than the amount mentioned in the notice of motion.
In addition, every taxpayer may deduct an optional standard deduction of $100 in lieu of claiming deductions for medical expenses or charitable donations. Every taxpayer may also deduct 3 per cent of his income from salary or wages, up to a maximum of $150. Taxpayers over 65 are granted an additional deduction of $650. The result of the combination of these deductions is that an employee with single status who is under 65 will not be subject to income tax until his salary or wage exceeds approximately $1,650. An employee with the full married exemption will not be subject to income tax until his salary or wage exceeds approximately $3,041.
The question is, what would be the effect on revenues if the high exemptions mentioned in the notice of motion were put into effect? Whom would we tax, or where would we obtain the needed taxes to overcome any losses. Of course, the tax reform bill passed last year provided for the imposition of capital gains taxes. These will supply additional revenues and allow tax levels to be reduced for practically all people in the labour force. Everyone pretty well, with the exception of single status taxpayers earning more than $8,500 a year, will benefit. Married couples with dependants will pay reduced taxes. As I say, the reductions will affect almost everyone.
The revenue implications of the hon. member's resolution cannot be easily estimated in detail. However, with starting points of $3,000 and $5,000 it would probably reduce revenues by less than $100 million, although this would depend substantially upon the notch provision used to tax income just in excess of the starting points. The increase in the basic exemption of the order proposed would cause substantial reduction in revenue. The order of magnitude can be guessed by noting that the increase in the basic exemptions from $1,000 to $1,400 and from $3,000 to $2,800, as proposed in the white paper on tax reform, was estimated at $1 billion.
When we look at this matter from the human point of view we cannot help but believe that what the hon. member is proposing will in the long haul be adopted in some form because of the inflation which occurs every year and the fact that people in the lower income brackets

will have less and less resources with which to pay taxes. This is the important point of a graduated scale: it not only helps the progressive tax system and the poorer parts of the country but it helps the poor people.
Last week a group from the national anti-poverty organization met in Ottawa. It presented briefs to all the caucuses of the House. I must say they were a very forwardlooking group. Like practically everyone coming to meet the government, they were looking for funds, but they were doing this in a positive way. They were looking for assistance in order to help themselves. This is an encouraging development.
This group proposed that there be a poor people's development corporation. Their proposal had two objectives: first, to assist income groups in developing self-sustaining organizations and, second, to allow low-income people to participate in some organizations. This corporation would be made up by appointments from the government and appointments from within their organization. The corporation would fund self-help projects.
One of the projects they proposed was co-operative grocery stores in isolated areas. They gave the example of a small community of 200 people in one of the western provinces which does not have any store to serve them. They suggested that this kind of national organization would be able to provide the resources for a self-help project. They also proposed that in urban areas funds be used for housing developments and that 5 per cent of the needed capital would be provided by this corporation: the balance would come from Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. This group also talked about free stores in Winnipeg, a self-help community organization. This would provide an opportunity to assist each other, as well as those who are transferred, in the provision of supplies.
I believe the motion before us would be of benefit to many Canadians in the lower income brackets. The idea of hearings on the tax reform measures which were before us last fall worked toward more growth in our economy. The budget that was presented last fall also worked in this direction. Personal income tax was lowered by 3 per cent and corporation tax by some 7 per cent in order to provide more funds to get the economy of the country moving faster.
I know there are speakers on both sides of the House who want to speak this afternoon. I think it is interesting that this debate should occur just at the time we are debating the federal tax sharing agreements which this afternoon received second reading, approval in principle. One of the beauties of this country is that we have such co-operation between the federal and provincial governments. We know that when the levels of minimum basic exemptions are raised to the levels suggested by the hon. member for Portneuf, they will apply across the country and the benefits will be nationwide. We do not have the tax jungle in Canada that we had at one time and which exists in many other countries.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
I congratulate the hon. member for Portneuf (Mr. Godin) for bringing forward this intriguing notice of motion. I would like to go on record as being sympathetic to the proposal of the hon. member if it really means relief to
March 3, 1972

Canada's hard-pressed taxpayers. However, as a responsible member of this chamber I must point out that having regard to practical considerations and a shrinking tax base that has not been recognized by the government, this probably would not bring the result that the hon. member envisages. I do not think for one minute there would be enough money left to go around. We are aware that next year income tax exemptions will be increased from $1,000 to $1,500 for single persons and from $2,000 to $2,850 for married couples, plus the $100 mandatory exemption. For married couples over 65 in standard circumstances where the wife is not earning any money, the exemption next year will be $3,600.
The notice of motion before us calls for the elimination of taxes for single people earning up to $3,000. This is an increased exemption of $1,500. In the case of married couples it calls for an increased exemption from $2,950 to $5,000, an increase of $2,050. These figures seem rather large at first glance but I suspect they are probably closer to the actual purchasing power of the dollar than the government is prepared to acknowledge. If one considers that until 1948 the exemption for a single person in this country was $750 and in 1949 it was advanced to $1,000, where it has stayed until today, and having regard to the decrease in purchasing power of the dollar during that time, I suggest that a fair figure might be 3 per cent annually, we know that it has been at least 4 per cent a year since 1966 and, therefore, having regard to the compounding effect of the decrease in the purchasing power of the dollar the suggestion of the hon. member is not so far out of line. Indeed, the Ontario Association of Superannuated Teachers passed a resolution along these lines regarding 1972 income tax exemptions. I have received dozens of letters from this organization and I should like to quote a resolution which was passed by them:
Be it resolved that:
(1)	The income tax exemption be increased for all citizens of Canada or 65 years and over to $3,000 for all single persons and $4,500 for all married couples, and
(2)	That an escalation clause be included in the exemption to establish an escalation geared to the cost of living for retired persons of 65 years and over.
These people are concerned, as well they might be. In light of the situation which exists I must say that while I am sympathetic to their case and to this resolution, in my opinion this approach is only a band-aid treatment for the disease: the cure for the disease is something else. I submit that the sky is the limit as far as exemptions go, but this will not treat the disease of profligate spending by governments in Canada today. This has placed our people in the unenviable position in which they find themselves.
I am not a senior member of the House by any means, but it came as a shock to me to find that in the short period in which I have been in this chamber the national budget has more than doubled. That is in less than a decade. No, Mr. Speaker, the answer is not necessarily to increase exemptions. I submit that the answer lies only in establishing real priorities for expenditures. The cure to this impasse is to spend money only on things which are worth while. We must cut out the frivolities. I ask this question: Has the group referred to as Satan's Choice or
Income Tax Exemptions
devil worshippers, or whatever they are called, which applied in Toronto for a LIP grant, actually received $25,000? If the money has been received by them, what is the situation? I make no statement as to whether they should or should not have received the money, but supposing after investigation it is determined that they should not have been given it: what happens? Do Canadian taxpayers have any chance of getting their money back? Has any taxpayer received a refund following the exorbitant waste in the course of refitting the Bonaven-ture"! What about the grant to CHAT, the Community Homophile Association in Toronto which received $14,602 to succour Toronto's homosexuals?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is indeed a pleasure to address a few remarks to the House on the motion moved by the hon. member for Portneuf (Mr. Godin). I suggest there is a great deal of merit in the hon. member's proposal by way of tax reform. It would result in purchasing power being placed in the hands of those who need it most.
I was interested in the comments of the hon. member for Algoma (Mr. Foster) who told us, with great piety, that he is sympathetic to the motion. Nevertheless, I note that the government which he supports, last fall when it had the opportunity to introduce meaningful measures of tax reform evaded its responsibility and put forward legislation designed merely to continue the special privileges of corporate interests. The government should take the opportunity afforded by this motion to alleviate the tax burden upon those whose incomes are low. The hon. member for Algoma told us that the government would lose revenue of $100 million. I believe this $100 million could be made up from sources of revenue other than taxing people of severely limited means.
The tax legislation introduced last fall left wide disparities in terms of what income is taxed and what is not. An individual who earns $10,000 a year as a farmer, a working man or a professional, will pay tax amounting to about $2,285. A person who derives an income of $10,000 from capital gains will pay in the neighbourhood of $788, and a person deriving a similar income from dividends will pay only in the neighbourhood of $173. Disparities of this kind are completely out of line with any concept of a just society.
It would be well for the government to allow this motion to go to a vote, assist in its passage and give a break to people in the low income brackets in terms of the tax they must pay.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have listened to this debate with considerable interest, particularly to the remarks of the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Knight) who has just spoken.

March 3, 1972
Income Tax Exemptions
I note that all members who have spoken have pronounced themselves in favour of increased tax exemptions, which is the basic principle embraced by this motion. They have also said that tax reform such as that already undertaken has not gone as far as it should have gone. I should like to raise one basic question for the consideration of the hon. member for Assiniboia. I believe in tax reform, in giving tax reductions to those in the lower income brackets; but when the hon. member increases the basic exemption by, say, even $1,000, then the man in the 80 per cent marginal tax brackets gets tax relief amounting to $800 whereas the man in the 20 per cent tax bracket gets tax relief amounting to $200. Therefore, I would ask him this question: Is this always the fairest and most equitable means of achieving the social purposes that I know he has in mind?
When one increases basic tax exemptions across the board there is no question in my mind that the greatest benefit from such an increase is derived by the man in the higher tax brackets.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have read the resolution very carefully and for the sake of the hon. member I will read it again into Hansard. The motion reads:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of introducing legislative measures so that the income of Canadians will be adjusted to the increasing cost of living-
How that is done, I do not know.
-by eliminating all taxes for single persons earning less than $3,000 and for married couples earning less than $5,000 with the addition of a further $500 exemption for each dependent child.
I agree there is some ambiguity of meaning, but there is reference to a further $500 exemption. Presumably an exemption is an exemption. Presumably this resolution is couched in terms of exemptions. Indeed, I find it difficult to read it in any other way. Is the resolution intended to give us an elaborate system of tax reduction that does not change the tax brackets of anyone except by a notch provision with certain starting points, such as was introduced by the province of Quebec in its administration of tax law?
I understand that in the province of Quebec the basic exemption for a single person is $2,000. The basic exemption under the new law would be something like $1,500 or $1,400, plus the $100 charitable deduction with the tax rate cutting in above that. Then there is a notch provision so that anyone paying taxes on, say, $501 would pay no more as a result of cutting in above the basic exemption.
It is not clear at all whether the Quebec system is intended here, or some blanket exemption. I personally read the resolution to mean there should be an exemption of $3,000 and one of $5,000.1 was not aware that the mover

of the motion made this point at all clear. I think my reading of it is consistent with the hon. member's remarks, but there will be other opportunities, I am sure, for members on all sides of the House to set the record clear.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
subtopic: INCOME TAX
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED INCREASE IN EXEMPTION LEVELS TO COUNTERACT INCREASED COST OF LIVING
speechtext:
I am delighted to hear that. One thing that is clear is that we have already gone through a measure of tax reform. We have increased basic exemptions. At the present time the law provides an exemption, for those claiming single status, of $1,500; and for those claiming married status, of $2,850. For each dependent child under the age of 18 eligible for an allowance there is a deduction of $300. For the dependent age 16 and over the allowance is $550. In addition, every taxpayer may deduct an optional standard deduction of $100 in lieu of claiming medical expenses and charitable donations.
Every taxpayer may also deduct 3 per cent of his income from salaries or wages up to a maximum of $150. Taxpayers over the age of 65 are granted an additional deduction of $650. The result of the combination of these deductions is that an employee with single status under age 65 will not be subject to income tax until his salary or wages exceed approximately $1,650. An employee with the full married exemption will not be subject to income tax until his salary or wages exceed approximately $3,041.
I want to make it abundantly clear that in the course of the inflation which unfortunately is part of our times, the case for a review of basic exemptions under our tax laws is so strong that it is unanswerable. The mover of the motion has given us no formula to relate this to the cost of living, despite the pious phrasing of his motion. It will be necessary to review the law from time to time and to raise exemptions in such manner as may be provided. But none of us is so naive as to think that this can be done without regard to the effect of increasing exemptions on tax yields.
I note, for example, that something like $1 billion was the estimated cost to the treasury of increasing exemptions from $1,000 to $1,400. Increasing them to $3,000 would result in a very substantial tax loss to the treasury. The cost of the $500 exemption for dependent children- and the word "exemption" is clearly used-would cost in the order of $500 million considered separately in its own right.
I am sure nothing will give hon. members on all sides of the House greater satisfaction than to be able to give tax reductions to large numbers of voters. I am sure that in this, an election year, the thought would be particularly appealing. But we have to be something more than just cynical in promising great things and large hand-outs; we have to ask ourselves the basic question: Is this the best way to administer expenditure for public purposes?
I start with the question I asked the hon. member for Assiniboia: Does he intend to give a man in the 80 pef cent tax bracket the greatest amount of tax relief? I am sure he does not. The effect of increasing exemptions in a blanket way would do just that.
